nameStory: The Lattice Tube Lichen gets its name from its unique hollow, tube-like lobes that create an intricate lattice pattern when viewed up close. Unlike flat shield lichens, this species forms distinctive curved tubes that remind observers of tiny architectural frameworks or delicate biological scaffolding.
description: Lattice Tube Lichen is a medium-sized foliose lichen that grows in rosette-like patches on tree bark and rocks. Its most distinctive feature is its hollow, tube-shaped lobes that curve and interweave to create a three-dimensional lattice structure. The lichen typically reaches 2-4 inches across and has a grayish-green to brownish color that can vary significantly between wet and dry conditions.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive hollow tubes that curve upward and inward, creating a complex three-dimensional lattice pattern rather than lying flat against the surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to brownish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; the underside is typically black with sparse rhizines (root-like attachments)

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth to slightly wrinkled surface that feels papery when dry and becomes more pliable when moist; the tubes feel hollow if gently pressed

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Most commonly found on bark of deciduous and coniferous trees, occasionally on rocks; prefers somewhat acidic surfaces

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies typically 2-4 inches across, with tube-like lobes reaching about 1/4 to 1/2 inch in length

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Rarely produces the cup-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) typical of many lichens; more commonly reproduces through soredia (powdery reproductive structures) found at lobe tips

habitat: Found on bark of both deciduous and coniferous trees throughout New England's forests, from sea level to moderate elevations. Prefers somewhat shaded locations with good air circulation and moderate humidity. Often grows alongside other members of the shield lichen family on oak, maple, pine, and fir trees.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant and noticeable as spring rains moisten the lichen, causing the grayish surface to turn distinctly greenish. The hollow tube structure is most apparent when the lichen is slightly damp from morning dew or light rain.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more grayish during dry spells, but the distinctive tube structure remains constant. Look for it in shadier locations where it retains some moisture even during hot weather.
seasonality.fall: Often easier to spot as deciduous tree leaves fall away, revealing lichen communities on bark. The tubes may collect small debris like tiny leaves or seeds, making the lattice pattern more obvious.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible and identifiable year-round, though it may appear more brittle when frozen. Snow can accumulate in the hollow tubes, creating an interesting contrast pattern that highlights the lattice structure.

funFact: The hollow tubes of this lichen act like tiny rain gutters, channeling water and nutrients directly to the growing tips where the lichen needs them most - essentially creating its own irrigation system!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other shield lichens that grow flat against bark, but the distinctive hollow, curved tubes immediately set Lattice Tube Lichen apart. Remember: if it looks three-dimensional with obvious tubes, you've likely found your lattice lichen rather than a flat shield lichen.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'tube lichen,' this species is actually in the shield lichen family (Parmeliaceae), showing how common names can sometimes be more descriptive of appearance than evolutionary relationships. The scientific name 'incurvoides' refers to the inward-curving nature of the tubes.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Hooded Tube Lichen which has more inflated, hood-like lobes, Lattice Tube Lichen has distinctly hollow, narrower tubes. Freckled Tube Lichen has tiny dark spots on its surface, while Powder-headed Tube Lichen produces more obvious powdery soredia at the tube tips. The lattice pattern of interwoven tubes is unique among New England's tube lichens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tube lichen relatives, Hooded Tube Lichen has those distinctive pepper-like black dots scattered across its surface and more pronounced upward-curling edges.

Freckled Tube Lichen differs from Hooded Tube Lichen by having scattered dark spots rather than smooth surfaces, and from Powder-headed Tube Lichen by lacking the powdery white soredia (reproductive dust) at the lobe tips.
Among the tube lichens in New England, Powder-headed Tube Lichen has the most inflated, balloon-like lobes compared to its relatives.
